questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain how divergence distinguishes a source from a sink
questions.stem: The divergence of a flow field tells you that one point in the tank is a source and another is a sink. Explain, in the tank notes, how it does so.

answer.exemplar: The divergence of a flow field at a point measures the net outflow per unit volume there. Where the divergence is positive, more fluid leaves a small ball around the point than enters it, so the point behaves as a source and the field spreads outward from it. Where the divergence is negative, more fluid enters than leaves, so the point is a sink and the field converges toward it. In the tank this shows up as the middle of a coral fragment releasing water while the filter inlet draws water in, and the two patterns can be told apart at a glance by whether the arrows point away from or towards the point.

questions.explanation: A good answer defines divergence as net outflow per unit volume, ties positive divergence to a source and negative divergence to a sink, and says the arrows point away from a source.
questions.hint: Divergence is net outflow per unit volume.

answer.exemplar: Dividing a total flux by the volume of the region gives the average of the divergence over that volume, because the divergence theorem turns the flux into a volume integral of the divergence. questions.learningObjective: Explain the projection of a tilted patch in Stokes' theorem
questions.stem: Stokes' theorem on a tilted patch depends on the projection of the patch rather than on its own area alone. Explain, for the tank notes, why.

answer.exemplar: Stokes' theorem states that the circulation around the boundary of a surface equals the surface integral of the curl of the field dotted with the chosen normal. When the curl is constant, that integral becomes the magnitude of the curl times the area times the cosine of the angle between the patch's normal and the curl direction. questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a conservative field has zero circulation
questions.stem: A conservative flow field has zero circulation around every closed loop. Explain, for the tank notes, why, and how you can check the claim in practice.

answer.exemplar: A conservative field is the gradient of some single valued potential function, so that the work it does along any path depends only on the endpoints of the path, not on the path itself. Travelling round a closed loop returns you to the same starting point, so the contributions along the loop must cancel and the circulation is zero. In practice one can check the field by differentiating its components and confirming the curl vanishes everywhere in the tank, and that the tank is simply connected so that no part of the field is hidden around the drain pipe.

questions.explanation: A good answer says a conservative field is the gradient of a single valued potential, so a closed loop contributes nothing, and mentions checking the curl vanishes on a simply connected region.

answer.exemplar: Stokes' theorem states that the line integral of a field around a closed loop equals the surface integral of its curl over any surface whose boundary is that loop. Instead of walking around the loop and sampling the field at every point, one may instead sweep the surface and sample the curl, which is often far easier because the curl of a simple field is a simple vector.
